title: Requirements Engineering for ML Systems
oneLiner: Before building a model, decide whether ML is the right tool, which business decision it will support, and how you will measure success.

what.html:
Requirements engineering for ML turns a business wish ("approve loans faster") into something you can build and check: the decision to support, the question a model must answer, the data it needs, and the measures that say whether it worked. Because ML output is probabilistic, requirements also say how much error is acceptable and how the model will be kept up to date.

Everyday versionBefore hiring a translator you decide which documents, how fast, for whom, and how you'll check quality. "Hire the best translator in the world" isn't a requirement; "contracts translated within a day with no legal errors, checked by a lawyer" is.

why.html:
• Many ML projects fail because they solve the wrong problem or chase the wrong number.
  • Some problems don't need ML at all; ordinary code is cheaper and safer when the rules are known.
  • A model's accuracy can go up while users get less happy and the business earns less.
  • You can't specify ML exactly, so goals and measures carry the specification instead.

how.title: Ask: is ML the right tool?
how.html: Use ML for problems that are intrinsically hard (understanding language), big (recommending from tens of millions of songs) or time-changing (fraud tactics). If the rule is known and stable, like tax rates or password length, write code.

how.title: Write data-aware, model-aware requirements
how.html: Ordinary software gives the same output for the same input; ML doesn't. So requirements must say what data is needed and how good it is, how the model should behave when unsure, and how it will keep learning as things change.

how.title: Line up goals at four levels
how.html: Organisation (grow revenue 20%), product (recommend relevant items), user (find products quickly) and model (high click-through rate). Goals can help each other (accuracy improves experience) or clash (accuracy vs speed, quality vs cost). Decide the priorities explicitly.

how.title: Go from goals to predictions
how.html: Find the decisions people make to reach a goal, ask which decisions a prediction would help, then check whether ML can make that prediction. Goal ← decision ← question ← prediction.

how.title: Business view: why
how.html: GR4ML is a way to draw this chain. In a bank, case workers want to process applications (measured by average resolution time). That needs a decision on each application, which needs the question "what is this applicant's credit risk?", answered by a credit-risk model retrained monthly on the last 48 months of data.

how.title: Analytics view: what
how.html: Decide the kind of analytics (here, classification), list candidate algorithms (SVM, Naive Bayes, decision trees) and the qualities that matter (accuracy, interpretability, robustness, coping with missing values). Each algorithm helps some qualities and hurts others, so record the trade-off.

how.title: Data view: how
how.html: Describe the data (applicant profile: age, balances, employment, existing credits, label) and the preparation steps: normalise, join, filter. Data engineers can then reuse and trust the prepared data. All three views together connect raw data to a business goal.

how.title: Choose good measures
how.html: A good measure ties to a goal, is objective and is practical to collect. It also needs to be accurate (right on average) and precise (gives similar answers when repeated). A leading survey question can be very consistent and still wrong.

demo.html: Explore one credit-risk project in three views. Start in the Business view and follow the chain from case workers to the model's settings. Then switch to Analytics design to see the algorithm trade-offs, and to Data preparation to see where the training table comes from.

example.html:
Chatbot for an insurance company. "Answer questions" is not enough. Organisational goal: cut call-centre cost 15%. Product goal: resolve common queries without an agent. User goal: get a correct answer in under two minutes. Model goal: intent accuracy ≥ 90% on a labelled set. Measures: task success rate, satisfaction score, conversation completion rate, handover rate. A conflict appears: a larger model is more accurate but slower, so the team caps latency at 2 seconds and accepts 88%.

Supplementary The same chain works for an agent: goal → decision ("issue a refund?") → question ("is this claim valid?") → prediction, with a human approval step for large amounts.

misunderstandings: The requirement is just a target accuracy.
You also need data requirements, error costs, slices, latency, retraining and a link to business goals.
Known, stable rules are better written as code.
Higher model accuracy always helps the business.
It can conflict with latency, cost or user experience.
It forces each prediction to be tied to a real decision and goal.
A precise measure is an accurate one.
A measure can be consistent and consistently wrong.
takeaways: Use ML for intrinsically hard, big or time-changing problems; otherwise write code.
ML requirements are measurable, data-aware and model-aware: data, behaviour under uncertainty, continuous learning.
Align organisational, product, user and model goals; make trade-offs explicit.
Goal ← decision ← question ← prediction; GR4ML captures this in business, analytics design and data preparation views.
Good measures relate to goals, are objective and practical, and must be both accurate and precise.
thirty: Requirements engineering for ML starts by asking whether ML is needed: it pays off for problems that are intrinsically hard, big, or changing over time. Because ML is probabilistic, requirements must be measurable, data-aware and model-aware, covering data quality, behaviour under uncertainty and continuous learning. Goals exist at four levels, organisational, product, user and model, and they can support or conflict, so trade-offs must be explicit. We go from goals to the decisions people make, to the questions those decisions raise, to predictions ML can supply. GR4ML models this in three views: business (why), analytics design (what algorithms and trade-offs) and data preparation (how the data is built). Finally, success needs good measures: tied to goals, objective, practical, accurate and precise.
